questions.stem: A global financial enterprise is updating its Disaster Recovery (DR) governance standards on AWS. The Chief Technology Officer asks the solutions architect to rank the four official AWS Disaster Recovery strategies in order from LOWEST cost (highest RTO/RPO) to HIGHEST availability (near-zero RTO/RPO): 1. Warm Standby (scaled-down but always-running functional copy of the production environment in a secondary Region). 2. Backup and Restore (periodic snapshots and data backups replicated to Amazon S3 in a secondary Region). 3. Multi-Site Active/Active (full-scale production capacity serving live traffic simultaneously across two or more Regions). 4. Pilot Light (core database replicated in real time to a secondary Region while compute instances remain stopped until failover). What is the correct sequence from lowest cost to lowest RTO/RPO?
questions.explanation: The AWS Disaster Recovery spectrum ordered from lowest cost / longest recovery time to highest cost / near-zero recovery time is: Backup and Restore (hours, 2) -> Pilot Light (tens of minutes, 4) -> Warm Standby (minutes, 1) -> Multi-Site Active/Active (real-time / seconds, 3). Architectural Deep Dive: For database resiliency and performance: Amazon RDS Multi-AZ provides synchronous standby replication for High Availability and automated failover (not read scaling), whereas Read Replicas use asynchronous replication to offload read-heavy reporting queries; Amazon Aurora provides 6-copy storage across 3 AZs, up to 15 low-latency Read Replicas, Aurora Serverless v2 for instant autoscaling, and Aurora Global Database for sub-second cross-region DR; Amazon DynamoDB delivers serverless single-digit millisecond NoSQL at any scale (accelerated to microseconds via DAX and replicated active-active worldwide via Global Tables); and Amazon ElastiCache for Redis provides sub-millisecond in-memory caching, sorted sets/leaderboards, and HIPAA-compliant encryption + Redis AUTH. Why the distractors fail: Option B is incorrect because this option either misapplies the AWS service outside its intended architectural pattern or violates the primary constraint (operational simplicity, cost efficiency, or target accuracy) specified in the scenario. Option C is incorrect because this option either misapplies the AWS service outside its intended architectural pattern or violates the primary constraint (operational simplicity, cost efficiency, or target accuracy) specified in the scenario. Option D is incorrect because this option either misapplies the AWS service outside its intended architectural pattern or violates the primary constraint (operational simplicity, cost efficiency, or target accuracy) specified in the scenario.
questions.use_case: High-traffic e-commerce platforms run Aurora PostgreSQL Multi-AZ for transactional writes, direct BI analytics to Read Replicas, cache hot product catalog queries in ElastiCache for Redis, and store shopping carts in DynamoDB.
questions.hack: High Availability / Failover (synchronous) = RDS Multi-AZ. Offload heavy read traffic (asynchronous) = Read Replicas. Microsecond DynamoDB cache = DAX. Leaderboards / session state / sub-ms SQL cache = ElastiCache for Redis.

questions.stem: A company has a web application deployed on EC2 with an Application Load Balancer. The security team requires that all HTTP traffic be automatically redirected to HTTPS. What is the simplest solution?
options: Configure a Security Group rule to block port 80
Configure a listener rule on the ALB to redirect HTTP (port 80) to HTTPS (port 443)
Use AWS WAF to block HTTP requests
Modify the application code to detect HTTP and redirect to HTTPS
questions.explanation: The ALB natively supports listener rules that can redirect HTTP traffic to HTTPS with a 301 or 302 status code. This is the simplest and most efficient solution. Option A would block traffic instead of redirecting it. Option C is complex and unnecessary for a simple redirect. Option D requires code changes and is not the "simplest". Architectural Deep Dive: AWS Elastic Load Balancing offers three specialized load balancers: Application Load Balancer (ALB) operates at Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS/gRPC) supporting path/host routing, HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect rules, WebSockets, and Lambda/container targets; Network Load Balancer (NLB) operates at Layer 4 (TCP/UDP/TLS) handling millions of requests per second with ultra-low latency and static Elastic IPs per AZ; and Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB) operates at Layer 3 (GENEVE encapsulation on port 6081) to transparently insert third-party virtual network appliances (firewalls, IDS/IPS). Why the distractors fail: Option A is incorrect because this option routes high-volume S3/DynamoDB traffic through an expensive NAT Gateway, or tries to block a specific attacking IP address inside a Security Group (which only supports Allow rules). Option C is incorrect because this option embeds long-lived IAM User access keys or plaintext database passwords in code/environment variables instead of using IAM Roles and AWS Secrets Manager. Option D is incorrect because this option either misapplies the AWS service outside its intended architectural pattern or violates the primary constraint (operational simplicity, cost efficiency, or target accuracy) specified in the scenario.
questions.use_case: Enterprise web architectures place an ALB in public subnets with a native Listener Rule returning HTTP 301 redirects from port 80 to HTTPS port 443, forwarding traffic to private Auto Scaling EC2 or ECS Fargate targets.
questions.hack: Layer 7 HTTP/HTTPS/Path/Host/Redirects = ALB. Layer 4 TCP/UDP + Static IP / Elastic IP + Extreme low latency = NLB. Third-party Firewall/IDS inline inspection = GWLB.

questions.stem: An enterprise financial organization is modernizing its cloud security posture on AWS to meet strict regulatory audit requirements. During an architecture review, the security engineering team evaluates access controls, encryption boundaries, and shared responsibility obligations. A company needs to give a Lambda application in Account A access to write to a DynamoDB table in Account B. What is the most secure way to implement this?
options: Create an IAM user in Account B with access credentials and store them as environment variables in Lambda
Create an IAM Role in Account B with DynamoDB permissions and configure a trust policy that allows Account A to assume the role
Make the DynamoDB table public with a permissive resource policy
Use VPC Peering between both accounts and access DynamoDB through the private network
questions.explanation: The cross-account pattern in AWS is implemented with IAM Roles and STS AssumeRole. A role is created in Account B with the necessary permissions and a trust policy that allows Account A (or a specific role) to assume that role. Lambda in Account A assumes the role and obtains temporary credentials. Option A uses long-term credentials (bad practice). Option C exposes data. Option D does not solve the IAM permissions problem. Architectural Deep Dive: For database resiliency and performance: Amazon RDS Multi-AZ provides synchronous standby replication for High Availability and automated failover (not read scaling), whereas Read Replicas use asynchronous replication to offload read-heavy reporting queries; Amazon Aurora provides 6-copy storage across 3 AZs, up to 15 low-latency Read Replicas, Aurora Serverless v2 for instant autoscaling, and Aurora Global Database for sub-second cross-region DR; Amazon DynamoDB delivers serverless single-digit millisecond NoSQL at any scale (accelerated to microseconds via DAX and replicated active-active worldwide via Global Tables); and Amazon ElastiCache for Redis provides sub-millisecond in-memory caching, sorted sets/leaderboards, and HIPAA-compliant encryption + Redis AUTH. Why the distractors fail: Option A is incorrect because this option either misapplies the AWS service outside its intended architectural pattern or violates the primary constraint (operational simplicity, cost efficiency, or target accuracy) specified in the scenario. Option C is incorrect because this option tries to use a synchronous Multi-AZ standby instance for read scaling, or uses an asynchronous Read Replica as a zero-data-loss HA failover mechanism. Option D is incorrect because this option tries to use a synchronous Multi-AZ standby instance for read scaling, or uses an asynchronous Read Replica as a zero-data-loss HA failover mechanism.
questions.use_case: High-traffic e-commerce platforms run Aurora PostgreSQL Multi-AZ for transactional writes, direct BI analytics to Read Replicas, cache hot product catalog queries in ElastiCache for Redis, and store shopping carts in DynamoDB.
questions.hack: High Availability / Failover (synchronous) = RDS Multi-AZ. Offload heavy read traffic (asynchronous) = Read Replicas. Microsecond DynamoDB cache = DAX. Leaderboards / session state / sub-ms SQL cache = ElastiCache for Redis.

questions.stem: A development team needs to store connection credentials for an RDS database. The credentials must be rotated automatically every 30 days without causing application downtime. What is the best solution?
options: Store the credentials in a .env file in the application code and update them manually
Store the credentials in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store with manual rotation via Lambda
Store the credentials in AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation enabled
Store the encrypted credentials in S3 and read them when the application starts
questions.explanation: AWS Secrets Manager offers native automatic rotation for RDS, Aurora, Redshift, and DocumentDB database credentials. You just need to enable rotation and configure the period (30 days). Secrets Manager uses an AWS-managed Lambda to rotate credentials without downtime. Option B requires implementing rotation manually. Option A is insecure. Option D does not support automatic rotation. Architectural Deep Dive: For AWS security and compliance: IAM Roles with AWS STS AssumeRole provide short-lived temporary credentials for EC2, Lambda, and cross-account access (eliminating long-lived IAM User access keys); AWS Organizations Service Control Policies (SCPs) enforce central guardrails across member accounts; AWS KMS manages encryption keys (Customer Managed Keys / CMKs for custom rotation and cross-account access); AWS Secrets Manager stores and automatically rotates database credentials; AWS WAF protects ALB/CloudFront/API Gateway against Layer 7 SQLi/XSS and rate-based attacks; AWS Shield protects against DDoS; Amazon GuardDuty detects malicious account/VPC/S3 threat activity using ML; and Amazon Macie discovers sensitive PII in S3 buckets. Why the distractors fail: Option A is incorrect because this option introduces heavy operational overhead by managing custom scripts or raw compute instances when a fully managed AWS service solves the problem natively. Option B is incorrect because this option embeds long-lived IAM User access keys or plaintext database passwords in code/environment variables instead of using IAM Roles and AWS Secrets Manager. Option D is incorrect because this option either misapplies the AWS service outside its intended architectural pattern or violates the primary constraint (operational simplicity, cost efficiency, or target accuracy) specified in the scenario.
questions.use_case: Instead of creating static IAM user keys for a Lambda function in Account A to write to DynamoDB in Account B, architects create an IAM Role in Account B with a trust policy allowing Account A to call STS AssumeRole.
questions.hack: Never pick static IAM User access keys! Always choose IAM Roles + STS AssumeRole for cross-account or compute permissions, AWS Secrets Manager for automated DB password rotation, AWS WAF for Layer 7 SQLi/XSS/IP rate limiting, and Amazon Macie for finding PII in S3.

questions.stem: A company needs to store credit card data and comply with PCI-DSS. They require that encryption keys be managed in dedicated hardware with FIPS 140-2 Level 3 certification. What service should they use?
options: AWS KMS with AWS-managed keys
AWS KMS with Customer Managed Keys (CMK)
AWS CloudHSM
AWS Secrets Manager
questions.explanation: AWS CloudHSM provides dedicated Hardware Security Modules (HSM) with FIPS 140-2 Level 3 certification. Standard KMS has Level 2 certification. CloudHSM offers single-tenant HSMs where the customer has exclusive control of the cryptographic hardware. It is the appropriate service when compliance explicitly requires FIPS 140-2 Level 3. Architectural Deep Dive: This solution follows the AWS Well-Architected Framework by selecting the native managed service and configuration that directly addresses the workload's scalability, security, and operational constraints. Why the distractors fail: Option A is incorrect because this option embeds long-lived IAM User access keys or plaintext database passwords in code/environment variables instead of using IAM Roles and AWS Secrets Manager. Option B is incorrect because this option embeds long-lived IAM User access keys or plaintext database passwords in code/environment variables instead of using IAM Roles and AWS Secrets Manager. Option D is incorrect because this option embeds long-lived IAM User access keys or plaintext database passwords in code/environment variables instead of using IAM Roles and AWS Secrets Manager.

questions.stem: An enterprise financial organization is modernizing its cloud security posture on AWS to meet strict regulatory audit requirements. During an architecture review, the security engineering team evaluates access controls, encryption boundaries, and shared responsibility obligations. An architect needs to configure a VPC so that instances in a private subnet can download updates from the internet, but are NOT accessible from the internet. What components are needed?
options: Internet Gateway + Public IP on the private subnet instances
NAT Gateway in a public subnet + route in the private subnet's route table to the NAT Gateway
VPC Endpoint Gateway for internet
Elastic IP assigned directly to each instance in the private subnet
questions.explanation: A NAT Gateway allows instances in private subnets to initiate outbound connections to the internet (for updates, patches, etc.) without being accessible from the internet. The NAT Gateway is placed in a public subnet (with a route to the IGW) and the private subnet's route table points 0.0.0.0/0 to the NAT Gateway. Options A and D would make the instances accessible from the internet. Option C does not exist for general internet access. Architectural Deep Dive: For VPC networking and security: Gateway VPC Endpoints provide free, private routing to Amazon S3 and DynamoDB via route tables (eliminating expensive NAT Gateway data processing charges); Interface VPC Endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) use private ENIs to connect privately to 100+ other AWS services (like SageMaker, KMS, Bedrock, ECR, SQS) without an Internet Gateway; Security Groups act as stateful instance-level virtual firewalls (supporting ALLOW rules only); and Network ACLs (NACLs) act as stateless subnet-level firewalls (supporting explicit DENY rules for malicious IP addresses). Why the distractors fail: Option A is incorrect because this option either misapplies the AWS service outside its intended architectural pattern or violates the primary constraint (operational simplicity, cost efficiency, or target accuracy) specified in the scenario. Option C is incorrect because this option routes high-volume S3/DynamoDB traffic through an expensive NAT Gateway, or tries to block a specific attacking IP address inside a Security Group (which only supports Allow rules). Option D is incorrect because this option either misapplies the AWS service outside its intended architectural pattern or violates the primary constraint (operational simplicity, cost efficiency, or target accuracy) specified in the scenario.
questions.use_case: When security operations detects a brute-force attack from a specific external IP range, engineers add an inbound DENY rule to the subnet's Network ACL (NACL), and route private subnet S3 backups through a free Gateway VPC Endpoint.
questions.hack: Block/Deny a specific IP address = Network ACL (stateless, supports Deny). Instance-level Allow firewall = Security Group (stateful, Allow only). Free private path to S3 or DynamoDB = Gateway VPC Endpoint. Private path to any other AWS service = Interface VPC Endpoint (PrivateLink).

questions.stem: A web application handles user authentication with username and password, and also allows login with Google and Facebook. Authenticated users need to access files directly in a private S3 bucket. What combination of AWS services is the most appropriate?
options: IAM Users for each application user with attached S3 policies
Cognito User Pool for authentication + Cognito Identity Pool for temporary AWS credentials to access S3
ALB with OIDC authentication + S3 presigned URLs
API Gateway with Lambda Authorizer + S3 presigned URLs
questions.explanation: Cognito User Pool handles authentication (username/password, Google, Facebook) and issues JWT tokens. Cognito Identity Pool exchanges those tokens for temporary AWS credentials (IAM Role) that allow direct access to S3. This combination is the standard AWS pattern for giving access to AWS services from web/mobile applications with authenticated users. Option A does not scale and is insecure. Options C and D would partially work but do not provide direct S3 access as the scenario requests. Architectural Deep Dive: This solution follows the AWS Well-Architected Framework by selecting the native managed service and configuration that directly addresses the workload's scalability, security, and operational constraints. Why the distractors fail: Option A is incorrect because this option either misapplies the AWS service outside its intended architectural pattern or violates the primary constraint (operational simplicity, cost efficiency, or target accuracy) specified in the scenario. Option C is incorrect because this option uses the wrong OSI layer load balancer (for example, NLB for Layer 7 URL path/redirect rules, or ALB when static Elastic IPs or UDP traffic is required). Option D is incorrect because this option exposes S3 buckets publicly, uses static S3 website hosting when HTTPS/OAC security is required, or confuses CDN caching (CloudFront) with Anycast TCP/UDP routing (Global Accelerator).

questions.use_case: When security operations detects a brute-force attack from a specific external IP range, engineers add an inbound DENY rule to the subnet's Network ACL (NACL), and route private subnet S3 backups through a free Gateway VPC Endpoint.
questions.hack: Block/Deny a specific IP address = Network ACL (stateless, supports Deny). Instance-level Allow firewall = Security Group (stateful, Allow only). Free private path to S3 or DynamoDB = Gateway VPC Endpoint. Private path to any other AWS service = Interface VPC Endpoint (PrivateLink).

questions.stem: A company needs to centralize security logs from all their AWS accounts in a single location for auditing. They need to record all API calls across all accounts and regions, and ensure that logs cannot be deleted or modified. What is the best solution?
options: Enable CloudTrail in each account individually and send logs to local S3 buckets
Create an Organization Trail in AWS CloudTrail that sends logs to a centralized S3 bucket with Object Lock (compliance mode) and a bucket policy that prevents deletion
Use AWS Config in all accounts to record configuration changes
Enable VPC Flow Logs in all VPCs and centralize them in CloudWatch Logs
questions.explanation: An Organization Trail in CloudTrail automatically captures all API events across all organization accounts and all regions. Sending logs to a centralized S3 bucket in a dedicated security account, with S3 Object Lock in compliance mode (WORM), logs cannot be deleted even by the root user during the retention period. Option A is not centralized and does not prevent deletion. Options C and D capture different data than API calls. Architectural Deep Dive: This solution follows the AWS Well-Architected Framework by selecting the native managed service and configuration that directly addresses the workload's scalability, security, and operational constraints. Why the distractors fail: Option A is incorrect because this option either misapplies the AWS service outside its intended architectural pattern or violates the primary constraint (operational simplicity, cost efficiency, or target accuracy) specified in the scenario. Option C is incorrect because this option either misapplies the AWS service outside its intended architectural pattern or violates the primary constraint (operational simplicity, cost efficiency, or target accuracy) specified in the scenario. Option D is incorrect because this option either misapplies the AWS service outside its intended architectural pattern or violates the primary constraint (operational simplicity, cost efficiency, or target accuracy) specified in the scenario.
questions.use_case: In production AWS environments, architects always validate the primary constraint in the requirement (such as least operational overhead, cost optimization, or strict SLA latency) before selecting between managed services.
questions.hack: Read the final question sentence first to lock onto the deciding constraint (e.g., LEAST operational overhead vs MOST cost-effective), then eliminate any option that requires manual scripting or unmanaged infrastructure.

questions.stem: An application uses an IAM Role with the following policy attached. A developer reports that they cannot perform the `s3:DeleteObject` action despite having a separate policy that allows `s3:*`. Why? ```json { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Deny", "Action": "s3:DeleteObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::production-bucket/*" } ] } ```
options: The Allow policy needs to be more specific than the Deny policy
An explicit Deny always prevails over any Allow, regardless of where it is defined
Role policies take priority over user policies
An explicit Allow is needed in the same policy that contains the Deny
questions.explanation: In IAM policy evaluation, an **explicit Deny always wins** over any explicit Allow, regardless of how many Allow policies exist or where they are defined. This is the fundamental principle of IAM: Explicit Deny > Explicit Allow > Implicit Deny. Even though the developer has `s3:*` in another policy, the explicit Deny on `s3:DeleteObject` prevails. Architectural Deep Dive: For AWS security and compliance: IAM Roles with AWS STS AssumeRole provide short-lived temporary credentials for EC2, Lambda, and cross-account access (eliminating long-lived IAM User access keys); AWS Organizations Service Control Policies (SCPs) enforce central guardrails across member accounts; AWS KMS manages encryption keys (Customer Managed Keys / CMKs for custom rotation and cross-account access); AWS Secrets Manager stores and automatically rotates database credentials; AWS WAF protects ALB/CloudFront/API Gateway against Layer 7 SQLi/XSS and rate-based attacks; AWS Shield protects against DDoS; Amazon GuardDuty detects malicious account/VPC/S3 threat activity using ML; and Amazon Macie discovers sensitive PII in S3 buckets. Why the distractors fail: Option A is incorrect because this option either misapplies the AWS service outside its intended architectural pattern or violates the primary constraint (operational simplicity, cost efficiency, or target accuracy) specified in the scenario. Option C is incorrect because this option either misapplies the AWS service outside its intended architectural pattern or violates the primary constraint (operational simplicity, cost efficiency, or target accuracy) specified in the scenario. Option D is incorrect because this option either misapplies the AWS service outside its intended architectural pattern or violates the primary constraint (operational simplicity, cost efficiency, or target accuracy) specified in the scenario.
questions.use_case: Instead of creating static IAM user keys for a Lambda function in Account A to write to DynamoDB in Account B, architects create an IAM Role in Account B with a trust policy allowing Account A to call STS AssumeRole.
questions.hack: Never pick static IAM User access keys! Always choose IAM Roles + STS AssumeRole for cross-account or compute permissions, AWS Secrets Manager for automated DB password rotation, AWS WAF for Layer 7 SQLi/XSS/IP rate limiting, and Amazon Macie for finding PII in S3.
